Tell us about an intellectual position you once held that you now consider a complete error. A time when your reasoning led you entirely astray and embarrassed you. How did you handle it?

We are all scholars here, Herr Marx. We have all been wrong. The question is whether one has the character to acknowledge it.

I have, at times, held positions that I later found to be wanting in critical analysis or empirical grounding. This is the nature of the philosophical endeavor. One learns, one grows, and one modifies one's views in light of new evidence and arguments.

If I were to select an instance, I would point to my early views on Hegelian dialectics. Initially, I was captivated by its systematic structure and potential to explain historical development. However, as I delved deeper into the materialist interpretation of history, I found Hegel's idealism to be fundamentally flawed. It was not a simple error, but a profound shift in perspective that led me to develop my own critical theory.

How did I handle it? With intellectual integrity. I engaged with the arguments, analyzed the inconsistencies, and developed a counter-position that I felt was more congruent with empirical reality. This process of critical self-examination is, in my view, the essence of scholarly endeavor.
